title: Irritable bowel syndrome (adult)
subject: gastroenterology
summary: Make a positive diagnosis from symptoms (Rome IV) after limited tests (blood count, CRP, coeliac serology, faecal calprotectin for diarrhoea), then treat by predominant symptom: soluble fibre, diet, peppermint or antispasmodics, loperamide or laxatives first; low-dose tricyclics, rifaximin, linaclotide and gut-directed psychological therapy second line.

sections.title: Recognise
items: Rome IV: recurrent abdominal pain on average at least 1 day a week in the last 3 months, with 2 or more of: related to defecation, change in stool frequency, change in stool form; symptom onset at least 6 months before diagnosis.
Subtype by predominant stool form on abnormal days (Bristol scale): IBS-C, IBS-D, IBS-M. Subtype guides therapy.

Alarm features that need investigation rather than a diagnosis of IBS: age 40 or more with unexplained weight loss and abdominal pain; age 50 or more with unexplained rectal bleeding; age 60 or more with iron deficiency anaemia or change in bowel habit; positive faecal occult blood test.
Other red flags: nocturnal symptoms, family history of colorectal cancer, coeliac disease or IBD, fever, abdominal or rectal mass.

sections.title: Limited tests (positive diagnosis)
items: All patients: full blood count, CRP or ESR, and coeliac serology.

Diarrhoea: faecal calprotectin (BSG: under 45 years) plus CRP to exclude IBD. Below 100 mcg/g is generally normal; 100 to 249 mcg/g: repeat off NSAIDs and PPIs; 250 mcg/g or more: refer for colonoscopy.
Do not routinely do stool tests for enteric pathogens, food allergy or IgG food testing, hydrogen breath tests or pancreatic function tests in typical IBS.

No routine colonoscopy under 45 without alarm features. Consider colonoscopy with biopsies for suspected microscopic colitis (female, age 50 or more, autoimmune disease, nocturnal or severe watery diarrhoea, NSAID or PPI use).
Nocturnal diarrhoea or previous cholecystectomy: test for bile acid diarrhoea (SeHCAT or serum 7-alpha-hydroxy-4-cholesten-3-one) where available.
Refractory constipation or symptoms of a pelvic floor disorder: anorectal physiology testing.

sections.title: First line (all subtypes)
items: Explain the diagnosis as a disorder of gut-brain interaction; an effective doctor-patient relationship improves symptoms, quality of life and adherence.
Regular exercise and first-line dietary advice (regular meals, limit caffeine, alcohol, fizzy drinks and insoluble fibre such as wheat bran).
Soluble fibre (ispaghula/psyllium): start 3 to 4 g daily and build up slowly to avoid bloating.
Second-line diet: low FODMAP diet for a limited period, supervised by a trained dietitian, with structured reintroduction according to tolerance. Gluten-free diets are not recommended.

Pain and cramping: peppermint oil or an antispasmodic. BSG suggests certain antispasmodics for pain; ACG 2021 recommends against antispasmodics for global symptoms, so use them as a short trial and stop if no benefit.
Probiotics: BSG allows a 12-week trial then stopping if no benefit; ACG suggests against them for global symptoms.

sections.title: By subtype and second line
items: IBS-D: loperamide titrated to effect (constipation, pain and bloating can limit use).

IBS-D second line: rifaximin 550 mg three times daily for 14 days, repeatable up to twice for relapse; or ondansetron 4 mg once daily titrated to a maximum of 8 mg three times daily (constipation common).

IBS-C: polyethylene glycol improves stool frequency but not pain; linaclotide 290 mcg once daily is the most effective secretagogue (diarrhoea common). Lubiprostone and plecanatide are alternatives where available.

Global symptoms and pain (any subtype): low-dose tricyclic, e.g. amitriptyline 10 mg at night, increasing by 10 mg a week to a maximum of 30 to 50 mg; continue for at least 6 months if it helps. Avoid in QT prolongation or bundle branch block.
SSRIs may be used as an alternative second-line gut-brain neuromodulator for global symptoms (BSG, weak recommendation).
Gut-directed psychological therapy (IBS-specific CBT or gut-directed hypnotherapy) for persisting symptoms; recommended when drugs have failed for 12 months, earlier if available.

sections.title: Refer to gastroenterology
items: Diagnostic doubt, alarm features, abnormal screening tests, or severe or refractory symptoms despite first-line treatment.
The patient requests a specialist opinion.
Severe or refractory IBS: review the diagnosis and manage with a multidisciplinary team (gastroenterology, dietitian, psychology).

sections.title: Special considerations
items: Review response to each drug after about 3 months and stop it if there is no benefit.
Combining neuromodulators (augmentation) in severe cases needs vigilance for serotonin syndrome.

India: where intestinal tuberculosis, giardiasis and tropical sprue are common, keep a lower threshold for stool microscopy and further investigation if features are atypical (weight loss, fever, anaemia, persistent diarrhoea).

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Diagnosing IBS in a patient with alarm features, or missing coeliac disease, IBD, microscopic colitis or bile acid diarrhoea.
Repeated colonoscopies and imaging in typical IBS, which reinforce illness anxiety.
Opioids for chronic abdominal pain, and unnecessary surgery; these cause harm in IBS.
Faecal microbiota transplantation for IBS outside trials (ACG recommends against).

drugs.name: Ispaghula (psyllium) husk
drugs.dose: Start 3 to 4 g daily orally, increase gradually as tolerated
drugs.notes: Soluble fibre; avoid insoluble fibre such as wheat bran.

drugs.name: Peppermint oil (enteric-coated)
drugs.dose: 0.2 mL capsule, 1 to 2 capsules orally three times daily before meals
drugs.notes: Heartburn is the common side effect.

drugs.name: Mebeverine
drugs.dose: 135 mg orally three times daily, 20 minutes before meals
drugs.notes: Antispasmodic for pain and cramping; stop if no benefit.

drugs.name: Loperamide
drugs.dose: 2 mg orally as needed, titrated to effect; maximum 16 mg per day
drugs.notes: IBS-D. Watch for constipation and bloating.

drugs.name: Amitriptyline
drugs.dose: 10 mg orally at night, increase by 10 mg weekly to a maximum of 30 to 50 mg once daily
drugs.notes: Second line for global symptoms and pain. Avoid with QT prolongation or bundle branch block.

drugs.name: Rifaximin
drugs.dose: 550 mg orally three times daily for 14 days
drugs.notes: IBS-D; up to 2 further courses for relapse.

drugs.name: Ondansetron
drugs.dose: 4 mg orally once daily, titrate up to a maximum of 8 mg three times daily
drugs.notes: IBS-D second line (off-label); constipation is common.

drugs.name: Linaclotide
drugs.dose: 290 mcg orally once daily, at least 30 minutes before the first meal
drugs.notes: IBS-C second line; diarrhoea is the main adverse effect.

sources.title: ACG Clinical Guideline: Management of Irritable Bowel Syndrome (Am J Gastroenterol 2021;116:17-44)
British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines on the management of irritable bowel syndrome (Gut 2021;70:1214-1240)
